conflicts.conflict: Three lead fixes rewrite the bare `dyn` local in LT-1/LT-48: J2-03 and J3-01 write `p: owns dyn Picker = owns Mine(items=[9]) if ... else owns Yours(items=[9])`, and J4-06 writes the Picker variables the same way. J5-08's lead fix keeps those lines ('The lines in [LT-1] and [LT-48] stay as they are') and instead adds a local to TYP-45's list: '`dyn I` alone is a parameter's or a local's type ... a local given a value made on its line views a temporary'. Both cannot be written.
conflicts.resolution: Take J5-08. Verdict 152 itself states the program: 'With `p: dyn Picker = Mine(items=[9]) if input() == "m" else Yours(items=[9])` and `show(p)`, a `Mine` prints `[9]`'. Keep from J1-17/J4-06 only the mapping of verdict 163's line: `renderer: runtime owns dyn Renderer = owns Gpu(pixels=[0]) if input() == "gpu" else owns Software(unused=0)` (TYP-45's `Box[dyn I]` -> `owns dyn I`). Both spellings are then legal: a bare `dyn I` local views a temporary, and an `owns dyn I` local owns. Drop J2-03 and J3-01 entirely, and drop J4-06's Picker rewrite.

conflicts.conflict: J2-02 A rewrites TYP-46's list as a property: '`using` follows every type whose value itself holds heap memory: the owner words, a class, and every standard collection ... The list becomes examples of the property'. 'The owner words' include thread_shared. J5-05 A says '`using` may not follow `thread_shared`', and J5's notes warn: 'Do not rephrase the list as "every type with heap memory of its own": that would let `thread_shared` back in'.
conflicts.resolution: Ask K05 (J5-05) first. Whatever K34 (J2-02/J5-09) decides is then written as the property minus thread_shared under J5-05 A, with the reason stated (principle 6: a thread_shared value's block must come from the built-in manager that every thread may give memory back to). Under J5-05 B, it is minus thread_shared with a one-instance manager that is not ThreadShared.

conflicts.conflict: Where a function's loan ends. J3-02 A: 'A loan stays the default; `owns` before a named function hands it over to any `owns` parameter, the library's included'. `thread.spawn(push_a)` is refused because the function is kept, and 'return xs.iter().map(owns h) works the same way'. J6-12 A instead draws the line by parameter kind: 'A function from a variable is still lent, with no word, to a standard function that takes a function as its function parameter (`for_each(h)`, `map(h)`, `retain(keep)`)'. By that criterion `thread.spawn(push_a)` (a function parameter) would be lent, and so would a returned `map(h)`, against J3-02.
conflicts.resolution: One rule for both: a function from a variable passed with no word is lent (verdict 150). A loan the callee keeps past the call is refused at the call, with the help `owns h` or `owns copy of h`. The kept cases are a thread (`thread.spawn`), an element (`push`) and an adapter returned or stored (`return xs.iter().map(h)`). `owns` hands the function over (verdict 147). `for_each(h)` and `xs.iter().map(h).sum()` stay loans. Reword J6-12 A's sentence to 'lent to a call that runs it during the call'.

conflicts.conflict: J4-05 A's whole reason is cost: 'Turning an object that already exists into one would make every object of its class pay the bigger header, or move it and cut its links'. J5-06 B, recommended in the same set, rests on the opposite fact: 'Where a view of `inv` is used across the line that shares it, `inv` is put in its block where it is declared: the same one allocation, made earlier'. A local shared later in the same function is visible to the compiler, so only that local pays.
conflicts.resolution: Decide K06 as one question. If J5-06 B, J4-05 B's outcome must say that the compiler gives `s` its 32-byte block where it is made. No other Settings object pays, and no link is cut. `s` keeps only what a thread_shared owner may do from that line (E7014 for a direct change). See the recommendation change for J4-05. If J5-06 A, J4-05 A's reason stands.

conflicts.conflict: The same contradiction (RC-1 allows `thread_shared x` before a local, while THR-1, OWN-13 and E7017 refuse it) is an owner question in J4-05 and a lead fix in J7-05. J4-05 found that 'E7017 comes from the redesign's rule R3 (run 4), which is not an owner verdict', and that verdict 103 'speaks only of `shares`'.
conflicts.resolution: Owner question (K06). J7-05's text is option A's edit and is written only if the owner picks A. See the reroutes.

conflicts.conflict: J6-02 rejects its own option B because it 'needs a second way of tracking links for this one rule'. J5-07 A introduces exactly that tracking: 'The compiler follows the link from where it was made, through locals, fields and calls, as it follows a view'.
conflicts.resolution: Ask K17 (J5-07) before K43 (J6-02). If J5-07 A, J6-02's comparison must be redone: B then costs nothing new and accepts read-only links into the cached data. If J5-07 B, J6-02 A's reason stands.

conflicts.conflict: J2-11 B removes the library name: 'One spelling, the safe cast that exists; `ref_to_ptr` goes'. J8-12 A builds on it and widens it: '`ref_to_ptr(body)` gives a class object's address as an `ObjectPtr[Body]` without ending `body`'. That is a third meaning of a name TYP-26 forbids programs to overload, the very hidden path J2-11 objects to.

Under J2-11 B it is the cast (`body as ObjectPtr[Body]`, the same rule as `ref T` to `*T`), and under J2-11 A a named function of its own. Never a third `ref_to_ptr` overload. conflicts.conflict: J7-02 rejects C because 'C leaves resources held for ever'. J7-01 B ('the compiler empties main's queue only at check points where this thread holds no lock, walks no list and keeps no view that a queued type's drop may take') has the same hole. A thread whose loop runs entirely inside a `with lock:` block (or always walks a list) never reaches such a point, so the queued drop waits until the thread ends, or for ever for a pool worker or main (THR-16: no drop runs once main returns).
conflicts.resolution: J7-01 B must state its bound in the draft. Either (i) the compiler refuses a loop of a thread that may hold queued values when the loop has no clash-free check point (E7018, naming the lock), or (ii) the queue is also emptied when the clashing lock is released. Then J7-01 B and J7-02 A together keep 'every queued object is ended within one job or one callback'.

recommendation_changes.from: A: refuse `thread_shared s` of a local (E7017), because 'Turning an object that already exists into one would make every object of its class pay the bigger header, or move it and cut its links'.
recommendation_changes.to: B: allowed, as `shares s` and `shares mut s` of a local are (RC-1, verdict 23). The compiler, seeing the sharing line in the same function, gives `s` its 32-byte thread_shared block where it is made (J5-06 B's mechanism). From that line `s` may do only what a thread_shared owner may (a direct change is E7014), and E7015 still checks that everything reachable is Send.
recommendation_changes.why: A's reason is untrue for the case asked. RC-1 limits it to 'a local of this function', so the compiler sees both lines and only that local pays, not every object of its class, and nothing moves. With the cost gone, A refuses a correct build-then-share program and gives one of the three sharing words a rule of its own with no reason left.
recommendation_changes.checklist: 2 (accepts the correct program), 5 and 6 (one rule for the three sharing words, the nearest being RC-1's shares-of-a-local), 7, 13 (no second model for thread_shared), 3 (no run-time cost: placement decided when compiling)

recommendation_changes.from: A: `left, right = ref mut samples.split_at(mid)`, one word before the value for both names.
recommendation_changes.to: B, spelled as the pair is spelled elsewhere: `ref mut left, ref mut right = samples.split_at(mid)` (or in brackets, `(ref mut left, ref mut right) = ...`, mirroring `exists as (ref mut a, ref b)`), with GRM-42's 'each word belongs to the one name after it' extended to assignment targets.
recommendation_changes.why: The language already has a spelling for several names out of one pair, each with its own word: `if pair exists as (ref mut a, ref b):` for get_pair_mut, the sibling of split_at, plus match patterns and loop names. A adds a second spelling (one word for several names) and cannot say that one half only reads.

recommendation_changes.from: A: '`using` follows every type whose value itself holds heap memory: the owner words, a class, and every standard collection ... The list becomes examples of the property.'
recommendation_changes.to: A, restated: `using` follows a type whose value owns heap memory of its own, stated as a property a program's own collection type can meet too, and not only the standard library's names. thread_shared is left out with its reason (K05, J5-05 A). Or, if the owner is to be offered the narrower list, the option says plainly that a program's own containers cannot take `using`.

recommendation_changes.from: A as worded: 'Each `+` makes one new String (one allocation and copy)'.
recommendation_changes.to: A, with C++'s rvalue rule: `+` reads a named String in place and makes a new one, while a left operand that is a temporary (a value made on the line, such as the result of another `+`) is extended in place and given back. So `a + b + c` makes one String, as C++'s `operator+(std::string&&, …)` does. No named value is ever handed over without a word.
recommendation_changes.why: As written, A costs one allocation and copy per `+` in a chain, where C++ costs one. The refinement keeps A's point (no hidden hand-over of a name; a temporary has no name to hand over) and matches C++'s speed. It applies to the merged J6-14 too.
recommendation_changes.checklist: 3 (as fast as C++), 4 (nothing written: a temporary has no owner to name), 13 (no hidden hand-over of a named value)

order_rationale: Memory safety first: data races and corrupted counts in safe code (K01-K03), use after free and dangling views (K04-K06, K09), memory corruption or NULL reads through the C boundary from safe code (K07, K08), drops running inside a held lock or a walk (K10), unsafe code reached with nobody vouching (K11), a lent function kept past its owner (K12), then the weaker safety cases (read-only memory written, the old layout under new code, races through C++ `mutable`, unchecked code before main, the read-only parameter promise: K13-K17). Next, what ordinary games, servers and tools meet most: string `+`, constructors with an init, worker results, C++ overloads, queue drains, locks in match, moving parts out, views in lexers, iterators, literals, equality, callbacks (K18-K31). Then less frequent library, FFI and parallel questions (K32-K61). Rare corners last (K62-K76). Dependencies are honoured: K05 before K34 (the `using` list's wording), K12 before K31/K53/K76 (call words for kept callbacks), K17 before K43 (link tracking), K51 before K52 (`ref_to_ptr`), K19 before K32, K21 before K47, K22 before K23, K26 before K62. Inside a cluster the primary is shown first and the other members are added as lines of the same program, so the owner still answers one question at a time.
